candidate_markdown:
# My Journey

I used to preach [Buddhist enlightenment](http://mindset.u-dont-exist.com/) a lot. But an old childhood wound could still hit and suddenly I was the same little kid again, even when the spiritual part of me felt completely free.

The way I picture it is almost stupidly simple. Imagine you're broke and starving, and your baby is starving too. *Understandable*: there is no food. Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you've got lots of nutritious munchies. But you're eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving. *Unforgivable.*

Nobody leaves a baby starving on purpose. I just didn't believe there was a baby. Inner-child stuff sounded silly to me until I could actually feel him. Then there was this little me actually hurting, and I could send some of the love I'd already found his way.

I think most people who chase spiritual freedom are also trying to get away from something painful in themselves, and a lot of it goes back to childhood. That's [spiritual bypassing](https://goenka.u-dont-exist.com/). Plenty of seekers and gurus do it too; I've written about the [Dalai Lama as one example](https://substack.com/@udontexist/note/c-245314772?r=5vdc6m). I did it too. It doesn't mean you're stupid or crazy.

Spending your whole life processing the wounded kid isn't freedom either. Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—love and happiness beyond the conditions of my life story. Maybe ordinary life already gives you enough love and meaning. Great. It didn't for me. Conditional love felt radically insufficient, so I kept looking for something deeper.

### Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away

If you still feel like a kid inside, somebody who seems grown-up can feel like salvation, and handing them the steering wheel can actually help for a while. But they can know things you don't and still be wrong about you.

Even [Pema Chödrön](https://pemachodronfoundation.org/product/taking-the-leap-book/) comes from a tradition where devotion to a teacher is a big deal, and she still says a teacher should “wean us from dependency altogether” and help us grow up.

If something in your life is actually dangerous, sometimes you have to leave or get practical help. Meditation can help with the pain while you're dealing with it. It can't replace getting out of danger, and calling the danger merely “your story” doesn't protect the kid from it.

Say you grew up learning that what you wanted didn't matter. Now you're finally figuring out what you think, maybe even learning to say no, and somebody tells you there is no self. Maybe years later that feels freeing. Right then it can sound like the old message all over again. Sometimes learning what you want and being able to say no has to come first.

If you tell a therapist, “No, that's not right for me,” and they say the disagreement itself is resistance, then how could you ever tell them they're wrong? Maybe they've misunderstood you, or maybe what they're doing just isn't right for you. They have to be able to hear that without turning your no into more proof that they were right all along.

Borrow adulthood. Do not surrender it.

My own case was weird. I was well-loved as a child, but from age twelve to twenty-six I was depressed and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world. [Loving-kindness (metta) meditation](http://love.u-dont-exist.com/) healed that depression almost instantly for me.

I wasn't lacking love. My parents had given me a lot of it. I found more in [Buddhist teachings—which, it turns out, also include inner-child self-love!](https://substack.com/profile/355021294-u-dont-existcom/note/c-297324975) and later in [loveyhuasca](http://soma.u-dont-exist.com/). Metta gave all that love somewhere to land.

But it didn't reach everything. A lot of the child stuff around my attachment to women was still there. When I later tried [self-directed inner-child therapy](https://youtu.be/yEWFjODXJbI?si=IXUqrhExojOm6Itm), it felt like I was making it up at first. I used San Pedro cactus and CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open; structured sessions with an inner-child therapist deepened it.

“Find the wounded child and love them” sounded simple until I tried it. A protective part could stop me before I even got close to the child. And when I did get through, sometimes I wasn't sitting with the child anymore—I was him. The three adult jobs from the map don't work too well when the adult has vanished, so I started looking for a way to have an adult there before I could reliably be that adult myself.
